pages.text: 3 Chapter 1Summary1.1 Financial crime is becoming more sophisticated and complex. We’re consulting on changes to our Financial Crime Guide (the Guide) to help firms assess and strengthen their financial crime systems and controls. 1.2 Financial crime causes wide-ranging harm: it damages lives and livelihoods, enables serious and organised crime, undermines trust in the financial system and weakens the wider economy. Tackling it is one of our priorities and requires a coordinated effort across industry, government, law enforcement and regulators. Firms are essential partners in that collective effort. Their work to detect, prevent and disrupt financial crime helps protect consumers and safeguard the integrity of the financial system. 1.3 The updates we propose are informed by insights from our supervision and wider developments. We want the Guide to continue to help firms understand our expectations, strengthen their financial crime systems and controls and support their efforts to detect, prevent and disrupt financial crime. 1.4 The Guide includes self-assessment questions and examples of good and poor practice drawn from our supervisory work and wider financial crime publications.1.5 The Guide does not contain rules nor impose any new requirements. We expect firms to have read and considered it, using it as well as their own their judgement to establish effective policies and controls.1.6 Firms should factor in the UK’s System Priorities to demonstrate how they counter financial crime risk. The System Priorities framework is developing with focus on delivering more through Public Private Partnership.1.7 For further information on how these changes aim to prevent harm and how the consultation aligns with FCA objectives, see paragraph 1.13 and Chapter 2.1.8 This CP should be read by:• all FCA financial crime supervised firms, including firms we supervise under The Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017 (MLRs), such as Annex I Financial Institutions and cryptoasset businesses.1.9 The CP may also be of interest to:• individuals and organisations working with firms subject to our financial crime and MLRs supervision• financial services trade organisations and professional bodies• any other parties interested in our financial crime supervision, such as non-governmental organisations working on financial crime prevention, or academics

pages.text: 4What we want to update1.10 We want the Guide to be clear, reflect our recent findings, and help firms identify and assess the right financial crime controls.1 .11 We propose changes to the following areas:Fraud: Updates to reflect supervisory expectations and lessons from our multi-firm work on authorised push payment (APP) fraud and money mules, responding to industry feedback for more guidance. Cryptoassets: From 25 October 2027, firms carrying out certain cryptoasset activities in the UK will need to be authorised by us under the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (Cryptoassets) Regulations 2026. The Guide will help firms meet our expectations when developing and maintaining financial crime systems and controls. Financial and trade sanctions: The UK’s sanctions regime has evolved since the Guide was last updated, and since the Office of Trade Sanctions Implementation (OTSI) was established. We propose to update this section to reflect these developments and include examples of good and poor practice drawn from our supervisory work.Proliferation financing: Supervisory work has highlighted the need for enhanced guidance on proliferation financing risks and controls, including further detail on our expectations for firms.Data security: We want the guidance to keep pace with today’s financial crime and cyber risks, data protection legislation, governance and crisis communication, and emerging risks associated with AI, synthetic identity fraud and digital assets.Financial crime system and controls: Clarifying our expectations for firms using Banking as a Service (BaaS) delivery models, including where services are outsourced, white labelled or provided through embedded finance partnerships.Money laundering and terrorist financing: Updates so that the Guide remains current and reflects developments in industry practice, such as electronic verification, third party tools and outsourcing arrangements, and clarifying the importance of co-operation and information sharing. Consequential changes: Updates to the Guide, including reflecting recent changes to the MLRs that came into force in June 2026, updating expired links and references (including references to European Union legislation), and refreshing case studies.1.12 Further details are in Chapters 2-3 and Appendix 1.

pages.text: 5 Intended outcomes1.13 The proposed changes are to help firms:• reduce financial crime: We want to make sure that firms and markets are not used for financial crime. These changes give firms guidance on how they might evaluate or set up their systems and controls.• maintain confidence in the financial system: Confidence in the UK financial system depends on firms preventing harm to the public. We have proposed changes so that the Guide continues to reflect our expectations, and protects confidence in and the integrity of the financial system.• protect consumers: Effective financial crime systems and controls protect consumers from harm. The proposed changes reinforce our expectations that firms maintain controls that are proportionate to the risks they face.Outcomes and measuring success1.14 We will evaluate the impact of the consultation by analysing engagement and feedback on the proposed changes.1.15 We will continue to update the guidance in line with our supervisory findings and publications. We also welcome feedback on chapters from stakeholders on chapters or areas not addressed in this CP that they consider we should focus on in future.Next steps1.16 We welcome your feedback on our proposed guidance in Appendix 1 by 24 December 2026.The specific questions for feedback are in Annex 1.1 .17 You can submit your responses via the form on our website. Your feedback will also instruct our future updates to the Guide.

pages.text: 6Chapter 2Proposed changes Fraud2.1 Fraud has significant financial and emotional consequences for victims. It also undermines security and trust in the UK financial system. In recent years, government, law enforcement, regulators and industry have stepped up efforts to tackle it. 2.2 We have assessed systems and controls for detecting and preventing authorised push payment (APP) fraud and money mule activity at Payment Service Providers (PSPs), including retail banks, and payments and e-money firms. We have heard repeated calls from industry for more guidance on fraud.2.3 So we propose making updates to Chapter 4 – Fraud. These will incorporate the findings of systems and controls publications, including:• Anti-fraud controls and complaint handing in firms (with a focus on APP fraud)• Proceeds of fraud – detecting and preventing money mules • Firms’ use of the National Fraud Database (NFD) and money mule account detection tools• Combating romance fraud – prevention, detection and supporting victimsOur updated guidance focuses on APP fraud and money mule systems and controls, to help the firms we regulate meet their financial crime obligations. The new section on APP fraud and money mules is structured around three areas: onboarding, monitoring and reporting. The updated guidance is focussed on APP fraud as the overarching typology and does not reference specific fraud types associated with APP fraud. To reflect this, we have incorporated the guidance on investment fraud into the updated APP fraud section and set out that firms should be considering the risks associated with different APP fraud typologies as part of its anti-fraud systems and controls. We remain committed to tackling investment fraud:• we have introduced the Firm Checker tool for consumers to check firms are authorised by us and have the permissions to provide the services they want before making investments• we publish the FCA warning list of unauthorised firms• we publish information to help consumers protect themselves from scams • we have led international action to stop illegal influencers putting consumers’ money at risk.

pages.text: 7 Onboarding • We expect firms to consider the onboarding checks that will help mitigate both the risks of fraud and of moving the proceeds of fraud.• We have shared examples of good and poor practice for onboarding. They include: –Good practice: where firms have built a holistic view of the customer, reviewed a range of sources to aid behavioural profiling, used fraud databases, identified customer vulnerability, and implemented checks to identify synthetic or counterfeit documentation. –Poor practice: failing to keep accurate records of onboarding checks, completing basic checks that do not inform a holistic picture of the customer, and only being aware of customer vulnerabilities after a fraud has occurred.Monitoring• Swift and proactive detection of unusual activity helps firms spot weaknesses in systems and controls that fraudsters might exploit. • We have included some potential APP fraud indicators, such as changes in behavioural biometrics, changes in expected account turnover, negative Confirmation of Payee (COP) results, creation of new payees with high value transactions, and customers using increasingly desperate tones in communications. • We have included some money mule activity indicators, such as including unexpected or unexplained deposits, rapid dispersal of funds, changes in dormant accounts, online banking credentials changing, and changes to device or contact details are inconsistent with the firm’s knowledge of the customer. • There are examples of good and poor practice for APP fraud and money mule monitoring. They include: –Good practice: monitoring inbound and outbound transactions, reviewing and testing transaction monitoring alerts, customer warnings, prompt investigation of money mule alerts, and policies and procedures for the firm’s response to money mules. –Poor practice: inadequate staff training to identify APP fraud or money mule indicators, lack of feedback loops on updates to systems and controls, a focus on outbound transaction monitoring only, failing to promptly implement new transaction monitoring alerts, and failing to review or assess the impact of customer warnings. Reporting • We expect firms to have policies and procedures for reporting instances of fraud to the authorities. Reporting on fraud data, as well as wider information sharing, at an industry level plays a key role in tackling fraud across the whole system. We encourage firms to contribute to data sharing initiatives, in support of the wider cross-system approach for tackling fraud. • There are examples of good and poor practice for APP fraud and money mule reporting. Our proposed updates will give examples of good and poor practice, helping firms implement systems and controls to prepare for applications.2.10 The 2025 National Risk Assessment ranked the risk for money laundering as ‘high’ and for terrorist financing as ‘medium’ for cryptoassets. The cross-border and fast-moving nature of blockchain and cryptoasset transactions make detection and enforcement uniquely difficult. Our proposed updates to the Guide clarify our expectations that firms adopt a risk-based approach to identifying and mitigating these risks.2 .11 Our proposed guidance includes:• Good and poor practice examples on the triggers for enhanced due diligence, reflecting the financial crime risks faced by firms engaging with cryptoassets. • Good and poor practice examples of how firms meet our expectations on systems and controls, such as for onboarding and monitoring, and the use of blockchain analytics for firms engaging in cryptoasset activities.• Further guidance on firms’ obligations for complying with the Travel Rule.2.12 We are reminding firms of our expectations on governance. We expect all firms, including start-ups, to proactively monitor and adapt their approach as their business grows and matures.2.13 In addition, we are proposing to add a self-assessment question to help firms consider whether their policies, procedures and staff training adequately distinguish between obligations under the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002 and the Terrorism Act 2000. Financial sanctions and trade sanctions2.14 All firms should understand how their business may be exposed to sanctions risk and ensure their controls are proportionate to that exposure. Our supervisory work has shown that they’d benefit from more guidance on assessing their exposure and testing their controls.2.15 We are proposing updates to Chapter 7 of the Guide to set out our expectations and examples of good and poor practice. In particular, we propose to cover trade alongside financial sanctions, reflecting developments in the UK’s sanctions framework including the establishment of OTSI.2.16 The updates are to help firms consider their exposure to risk from their customers, counterparties, intermediaries, jurisdictions, goods, services, transactions, payments and payment messages. The guidance will help them assess their risk assessments, customer due diligence (CDD), screening, monitoring and reporting.

pages.text: 102 .17 We propose to update references to relevant authorities. The revised chapter will refer to OFSI for financial sanctions, OTSI for trade sanctions, HMRC where suspected breaches relate to export controls or customs matters, and to us where issues may indicate weaknesses in a firm’s financial crime systems and controls.2.18 The revised chapter will improve guidance on governance, management information, risk assessment, CDD, screening, evasion detection, asset freezing, licensing and breach reporting. It will reorganise some existing material so that the chapter is easier to follow and refreshed with more recent FCA enforcement examples.2.19 The specific guidance includes:• Explaining how firms may be exposed to financial and trade sanctions risk through their business relationships, activities and transaction flows.• Clarifying the respective roles of OFSI, OTSI, HMRC and the FCA, including the circumstances in which matters may need to be reported to each authority.• Strengthening guidance on governance and management information, including senior management oversight, escalation, training and the monitoring of sanctions controls.• Expanding risk assessment guidance to address matters such as sanctions circumvention, intermediary countries and sectoral and trade sanctions.• Enhancing guidance on CDD and KYC, including the consideration of ownership structures, connected parties, counterparties and relevant trade information.• Reorganising the screening material to distinguish more clearly between screening policies, sanctions-list management, system calibration, testing and alert management.• Clarifying firms’ responsibilities when using third-party screening tools or outsourced arrangements, including oversight of vendor-configured settings and the timely, complete and accurate implementation of sanctions-list data.• Encouraging firms to consider monitoring beyond name screening, including risks associated with goods, vessels, ports, services and jurisdictions.• Developing guidance on detecting sanctions evasion through appropriate typologies, data analysis, thematic review and transaction monitoring.• Setting out practices for managing screening alerts, including resourcing, backlogs, internal decision-making standards and audit trails.• Updating guidance on asset freezing, licensing and suspected breaches, including escalation, root cause analysis and reporting to the relevant authorities.

pages.text: 11 Proliferation financing 2.20 We propose to update the proliferation financing material in Chapter 7. The revisions recognise that proliferation financing may involve mechanisms similar to sanctions evasion and clarifies how firms might manage the risk through existing controls.2.21 We propose to add self-assessment questions and examples of good and poor practice covering strategic export controls, dual-use and military goods, reporting and escalation procedures, the integration of proliferation financing into risk assessments, and how firms respond to published typologies when assessing their exposure to proliferation financing risks.2.22 It includes: • explaining how sanctions controls may help manage proliferation financing risk• guidance on higher-risk goods and activities, including strategic export controls, dual-use goods and military goods • guidance on documented reporting and escalation procedures for suspected proliferation financing breaches• updated good practice examples such as integrating proliferation financing risk into risk assessments, reviewing exposure after typology publications, and avoiding failures to incorporate PF risk into onboarding, CDD, screening and transaction monitoring. We also included examples of poor practice 2.23 In addition, if a new Proliferation Finance National Risk Assessment is published before we have finalised the Guide, we’ll include a reference to it. Data security2.24 We propose to update the Data Security guidance, so it reflects today’s financial crime and cyber risk landscape. Changes include:• updating outdated legislative references to align with the Data Protection Act 2018 and UK GDPR• strengthening governance expectations by incorporating board involvement, improved crisis communication; and• refreshing self-assessment material covering AI, synthetic identity fraud and digital asset-related risk 2.25 This will help firms assess whether their systems and controls are effective. The case studies and the ‘five fallacies of data loss and identify fraud’ section will be refreshed to reflect modern threats, including deepfakes. We’ll include learnings from recent enforcement cases, so that firms can benchmark themselves against risks.

pages.text: 12Financial crime systems and controls2.26 We propose to set out how financial crime obligations apply in Banking as a Service (BaaS) and embedded finance arrangements, both where the BaaS user is another regulated firm and where it is unregulated. The guidance reinforces that regulated firms are accountable for maintaining effective systems and controls across the delivery chain, including where activities are outsourced, white-labelled or delivered through embedded finance models.Money laundering and terrorist financing 2.27 Firms are increasingly using AI and other third-party tools in their financial crime systems and controls. They must apply governance and oversight to these and remain accountable for managing the financial crime risks they present. The tools must be proportionate to the firm’s risk profile and risk appetite, and subject to testing and validation. 2.28 We are proposing additions to the Guide so that it remains current and aligned with industry practice, such as expanded guidance on electronic verification. We have added examples of good and poor practice relating to notification obligations for PSPs and Intermediary Service Providers where there are repeated failures to comply with fund transfer requirements involving electronic transmission. We have also updated related terminology, including replacing references to Production Orders with Investigative Court Orders. 2.29 The banking and financial sector is critical national infrastructure, relied upon by businesses and the public every day. We have a duty to promote the resilience of the sector and its ability to withstand attempts to disrupt or deny services. We work closely with law enforcement agencies, regulators and other authorities to support stable, resilient and robust financial systems, maintained by effective co-operation and information sharing. We therefore propose to reinforce the importance of this between firms, regulators, law enforcement agencies and other relevant authorities.Consequential changes 2.30 We are proposing other changes to keep the Guide up to date, as a consequence of wider changes. These are:• Updating it to reflect amendments to the MLRs introduced in June 2026.• Removing references to European Union rules and supervisory authorities to keep it consistent with changes following the UK’s exit from the EU.• Refreshing links and more recent examples of outcomes on financial crime.• Including more links to useful material for firms to consult when conducting or reviewing their systems and controls.• Making other minor drafting changes.

pages.text: 16Annex 2Cost benefit analysisIntroduction1. The Financial Services and Markets Act (2000) require us to publish a cost benefit analysis (CBA) of our proposed rules. Specifically, section 138I requires us to publish a CBA of proposed rules, defined as ‘an analysis of the costs, together with an analysis of the benefits that will arise if the proposed rules are made’. 2. However, FSMA does not require us to produce and publish a CBA when proposing guidance (see section 139A of FSMA on power of the FCA to give guidance and section 139B of FSMA on the meaning of general guidance). As set out in our Statement of Policy on CBAs we may produce a CBA for general guidance if a high-level assessment of the impact of the proposal identifies an element of novelty, which may be in effect prescriptive or prohibitive, that may result in significant costs being incurred.3. Our Statement of Policy on CBAs provides that a CBA is undertaken where changes to guidance are likely to result in significant costs. In this case, we do not consider that significant costs will arise. The proposed updates reflect existing regulatory expectations and established industry practice and are intended to clarify and update existing guidance, not introduce new requirements. We therefore do not expect the proposals to result in a material increase in the frequency of, or time spent on, compliance activities, nor do we expect them to result in material costs to consumers, materially alter the products and services provided by firms, or have a material impact on competition or the wider economy.4. The proposals in this consultation relate to general guidance as defined in section 139B of FSMA. As explained in FCG 1.1.7, the Guide contains general guidance that is not binding and a firm’s departure from that guidance does not, of itself, indicate a breach of FCA rules. Therefore, we have not undertaken a CBA.

This Annex records the FCA’s compliance with a number of legal requirements applicable to the proposals in this consultation, including an explanation of the FCA’s reasons for concluding that our proposals in this consultation are compatible with certain requirements under the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (FSMA). 2. Section 1B(1) of FSMA requires that the FCA, when discharging its general functions, as far as reasonably possible, act in a way which is compatible with its strategic objective and advances one or more of its operational objectives, and its general duty under section 1B(5)(a) of FSMA to have regard to the regulatory principles in section 3B of FSMA.3. This Annex also sets out the FCA’s view of how the proposed rules are compatible with the duty on the FCA to discharge its general functions (which include rule-making) in a way which promotes effective competition in the interests of consumers (section 1B(4)). This duty applies in so far as promoting competition is compatible with advancing the FCA’s consumer protection and/or integrity objectives. 4. In addition, we have considered the recommendations made by the Treasury under s 1JA FSMA about aspects of the economic policy of His Majesty’s Government to which we should have regard in connection with our general duties. 5. pages.text: 18the UK’s financial sector and its reputation internationally. The guidance set out in this CP helps to ensure that firms can be confident they are fulfilling their obligations with regards to AML, Counter Terrorist Financing (CTF), sanctions and PF, while also allowing firms to take an innovative, technology-led approach if they wish. Firms that utilise innovative solutions will be able to reinvest their efficiency savings in productive areas of their businesses, facilitating economic growth.9. In preparing the proposals set out in this consultation, the FCA has had regard to the regulatory principles set out in s 3B FSMA of:The need to use our resources in the most efficient and economic way10. Publishing our regulatory findings and providing feedback and communication to the industry on financial crime systems and controls is a cost-effective way of using our resources. FCA applies a risk-based approach to supervision, targeting more of our resource to where risk is greater and deploying a range of tools, including providing guidance to firms. With guidance we can communicate, in addition to other publications, our supervisory findings, including on those firms at higher risk.The principle that a burden or restriction should be proportionate to the benefits11 . As set out in Annex 2, we do not expect the proposals to result in significant costs and, accordingly, we have not undertaken a CBA. The need to contribute towards achieving compliance by the Secretary of State with section 1 of the Climate Change Act 2008 (UK net zero emissions target) [and section 5 of the Environment Act 2021 (environmental targets)]]12. We have considered the environmental, social and governance (ESG) implications of our proposals, including our duty under sections 1B(5) and 3B(c) of FSMA to have regard to contributing towards the Secretary of State achieving compliance with the net-zero emissions target under section 1 of the Climate Change Act 2008 and environmental targets under section 5 of the Environment Act 2021. While we do not consider these proposals to be relevant to those targets, we welcome consultation feedback on any ESG implications.

However, through better financial crime controls at firms that consumers use, we believe that The Guide and better guidance will result indirectly in better consumer outcomes and protection.The responsibilities of senior management in relation to compliance with requirements imposed under FSMA, especially where they relate to consumers14. The consultation does not propose changes to the responsibilities of senior management.The desirability of exercising our functions in a way that recognises the differences in the nature of - and objectives of - businesses carried on by different persons including mutual societies and other kinds of business organisation15. The consultation is proposing changes as guidance only. A business can have regard to the guidance as it sees fit.The desirability of publishing information relating to persons subject to requirements imposed under FSMA, or requiring them to publish information to advance our [operational and secondary] objectives 16. This consultation is aligned with these objectives. It is providing further information to firms subject to FSMA Financial Crime Rules.The responsibilities of senior management17. The consultation does not propose changes to the responsibilities of senior management.The principle that we should exercise of our functions as transparently as possible18. The consultation is aligned with this objective and provides transparent communication on our proposals to the firms we supervise.19. In formulating these proposals, the FCA has had regard to the importance of taking action intended to minimise the extent to which it is possible for a business carried on (i) by an authorised person or a recognised investment exchange; or (ii) in contravention of the general prohibition, to be used for a purpose connected with financial crime (as required by s 1B(5)(b) FSMA).

pages.text: 20Expected effect on mutual societies20. The FCA does not expect the proposals in this paper to have a significantly different impact on mutual societies.Compatibility with the duty to promote effective competition in the interests of consumers 21. In preparing the proposals as set out in this consultation, we have had regard to the FCA’s duty to promote effective competition in the interests of consumers. This is set out in paragraphs 1.13 of the consultation paper.Equality and diversity 22. We have considered the equality and diversity issues that may arise from these and concluded that they do not materially impact any of the groups with protected characteristics under the Equality Act 2010. But we will continue to consider the equality and diversity implications of the proposals during the consultation period and will revisit them when finalising our guidance.Legislative and Regulatory Reform Act 2006 (LRRA)23. Under the Legislative and Regulatory Reform Act 2006 (LRRA) the FCA is subject to requirements to have regard to a number of high-level ‘Principles’ in the exercise of some of our regulatory functions and to have regard to a ‘Regulators’ Code’ when determining general policies and principles and giving general guidance (but not when exercising other legislative functions like making rules).24. These principles are that regulatory activities should be carried out in a way which is: • transparent • accountable • proportionate • consistent and • targeted only at cases in which action is needed25. The proposals in the CP are aimed to help ensure effective compliance in the firms we supervise. By publishing good and poor practice and our supervisory findings in The Guide, we are providing firms with more detailed guidance on our expectations and the outcomes we want to see. We note that The Guide is for guidance only and firms should use a risk-based approach. There are no rule changes, the proposals are proportionate and aimed at assisting the supervised firms.

pages.text: FCA 202X/YY Page 8 of 67 3.2.4 ... Firms are required to collect proof of company registration (or an excerpt from the register) before establishing a business relationship with certain legal entities including a company subject to the requirements of Part 21A of the Companies Act 2006, a limited liability partnership or an eligible Scottish partnership. Firms are required to report to Companies House material discrepancies between this information and information which otherwise becomes available to them in the course of complying with the Money Laundering Regulations. Firms may wish to refer to further guidance from the Companies House. Firms only need to report to Companies House in case of a material discrepancy. Schedule 3AZA (Material Discrepancies) of the Money Laundering Regulations defines a material discrepancy. Where a firm provides a customer with a pooled client account, it should have regard to the requirements in regulation 29 (Additional customer due diligence measures: credit institutions and financial institutions) of the Money Laundering Regulations, including taking the steps set out in regulation 29(11) to (17), where applicable. Specific CDD requirements apply where a customer opening an account is an insolvent banking customer. Firms should have regard to regulation 30ZA (Insolvent bank customers) of the Money Laundering Regulations. ... Firms should note that an electronic identification process tools and the use of digital identity solutions may be regarded as a reliable source sources for the purposes of CDD verification where that process is they are independent of the person whose identity is being verified, secure from against fraud and misuse and capable of providing an appropriate level of assurance that the person claiming a particular identity is in fact that person with that identity. Firms using digital identities as part of their CDD should have regard to the government’s guidance on using digital identities under the Money Laundering Regulations. A UK-authorised stablecoin issuer, or a third party carrying out the AML checks on its behalf, should conduct CDD checks within a reasonable timeframe during onboarding and redemption, while ensuring compliance with its obligations under regulations 27 (Customer due diligence) and 28 (Customer due diligence measures) of the Money Laundering Regulations. Redemption should only occur once relevant financial crime obligations have been complied with. Authorised cryptoasset firms and cryptoasset businesses should also consider how technology can be used, where appropriate, to support CDD, EDD and ongoing monitoring, such as to identify cloned documentation, identify engagement with higher risk products and/or services, and otherwise enable them to fulfil their financial crime obligations. Where a firm uses third-party tools or services to support key elements of its CDD or transaction monitoring processes, it remains responsible for ensuring that appropriate oversight and governance arrangements are in place to ensure that regulatory requirements and responsibilities are met.

pages.text: FCA 202X/YY Page 12 of 67 JMLSG guidance sets out how firms should apply EDD in differing correspondent trading relationships. • Politically exposed persons (PEPs), family members and known close associates of a PEP: a PEP is a person entrusted with a prominent public function, other than as a middle-ranking or more junior official. PEPs (as well as their family members and known close associates) must be subject to enhanced scrutiny. A senior manager at an appropriate level of authority must also approve the initiation of a business relationship with a PEP (or with a family member, or known close associate, of a PEP). This includes approving a relationship continuing with an existing customer who became a PEP after the relationship begun. In meeting these obligations firms may have regard to the FCA’s guidance on a risk-based approach to PEPs. Regulation 35(3A) (Enhanced customer due diligence: politically exposed persons) of the Money Laundering Regulations also provides that the starting point for the risk assessment is that a domestic PEP, or a family member or known close associate of a domestic PEP, presents a lower level of risk than a non-domestic PEP. • Business relationships or a ‘relevant transaction’ where either party is established in a high risk third country FATF call for action country: the Money Laundering Regulations defines define: (a) a high-risk third country as a country named by FATF on in FATF’s list of High-Risk Jurisdictions subject to a Call for Action or its list of Jurisdictions under Increased Monitoring; ... ... • Other transactions: EDD must be performed: (a) in any case where a transaction is unusually complex or unusually large (having regard to the nature of the transaction), or there is an unusual pattern of transactions, or the transaction or transactions have no apparent economic or legal purpose. In this scenario, there are specified EDD measures which must include, as far as reasonably possible, examining the background and purpose of the transaction and increasing the degree and nature of monitoring of the business relationship in which the transaction is made to determine whether that transaction or that relationship appears to be suspicious; (b) ... (c) where findings from blockchain analysis indicates exposure to criminal or sanctioned activities. In these circumstances, firms should consider how their AML policies, controls and procedures should be strengthened where they are exposed to non-UK-issued qualifying stablecoins, particularly where the regulatory treatment of those stablecoins differs from that in the UK. ...

pages.text: FCA 202X/YY Page 18 of 67 • FCA statement: www.fca.org.uk/news/statements/fca-sets-out-expectations-ukcryptoasset-businesses-complying-travel-rule FCA statement on cryptoasset travel rule • FCA guidance on payment service providers ... 4 Fraud 4.1 Introduction ... 4.1.3 The contents of FCG’s fraud chapter reflect the FSA’s previous thematic work in this area, as well as the FCA’s publications in relation to authorised push payment (APP) fraud and money mule activity. This means it does not specifically address such topics as plastic card unauthorised fraud, cheque or insurance fraud. This is not because the FCA regards fraud prevention of these topics as unimportant. Rather it reflects our view that our limited resources are better directed elsewhere, given the strong incentive firms should have to protect themselves from fraud; and the number of other bodies active in fraud prevention. Links to some of these other bodies are provided in FCG 4.4. the existing incentives and liability protections in place for certain types of fraud, as well as the extensive landscape of policies and initiatives designed to incentivise and support firms to improve their detection and prevention of fraud. This guidance supports the cross-system approach required to tackle fraud and reflects that our resources have been directed towards topics such as APP fraud (including investment fraud) and money mule activity. 4.1.4 The Failure to Prevent Fraud offence was introduced as part of the Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act 2023 (ECCTA 2023) and came into force on 1 September 2025. Under ECCTA 2023, an organisation may be criminally liable where an employee, agent, subsidiary undertaking or other ‘associated person’ commits a fraud intending to benefit the organisation and the organisation did not have reasonable fraud prevention procedures in place. The Home Office has issued guidance to organisations, which is supported by sector-specific guidance published by UK Finance. The FCA does not enforce or give guidance on the Failure to Prevent Fraud Offence under ECCTA 2023. But: • firms which are subject to SYSC 3.2.6R and SYSC 6.1.1R are under a separate regulatory obligation to establish and maintain effective systems and controls to mitigate financial crime risk. A breach of the Failure to Prevent Fraud Offence may impact upon a firm’s compliance with these SYSC rules; and • e-money institutions and payment institutions must satisfy us that they have robust governance, effective risk procedures and adequate internal control mechanisms. See regulation 6 of the Electronic Money Regulations and regulation 6 of the Payment Services Regulations.

pages.text: FCA 202X/YY Page 19 of 67 4.2 Themes Preventing losses from fraud 4.2.1 All firms will wish to protect themselves and their customers from fraud. Management oversight, risk assessment and fraud data will aid this, as will tailored controls on the ground. We expect a firm to consider the full implications of the breadth of fraud risks it faces, including the risk that it is used to move the proceeds of fraud, which may have wider effects on its reputation, its customers and the markets in which it operates. The general guidance in FCG 2 also applies in relation to fraud. We expect a firm to place sufficient focus on ensuring customers do not become victims of fraud and that the firm is not being exploited by fraudsters to move the proceeds of fraud. The topics outlined in FCG 4.2 provide detail on our expectations for firms’ anti-fraud prevention systems and controls. In addition to the guidance set out in this section, firms should consider how the self-assessment questions and good and poor practice examples set out FCG 2.2 (Themes) can be applied to fraud. ... Examples of good practice Examples of poor practice • The firm takes a view on what areas of the firm are most vulnerable to fraudsters, and tailors defences accordingly • Senior management appear unaware of fraud incidents and trends. No management information is produced. • Controls adapt to new fraud threats. • Fraud losses are buried in bad debts or other losses. • The firm engages with relevant cross-industry efforts to combat fraud (e.g. data-sharing initiatives like CIFAS and the Insurance Fraud Bureau, collaboration to strengthen payment systems, etc.) in relation to both internal and external fraud. • There is no clear and consistent definition of fraud across the business, so reporting is haphazard. • Fraud response plans and investigation procedures set out how the firm will respond to incidents of fraud. • Fraud risks are not explored when new products and delivery channels are developed. • Lessons are learnt from incidents of fraud. • Staff lack awareness of what constitutes fraudulent behaviour

Management information (MI) 4.2.1B MI should provide senior management with sufficient information to understand the fraud risks to which their firm is exposed. MI should be provided regularly and ad hoc, to help senior management adhere to its own fraud risk appetite, to effectively manage fraud risks and to improve systems and controls. Examples of fraud MI can include but are not limited to: • rates of fraud detected; • rates of fraud prevented; • rates of false positive fraud alerts detected; • the volumes and value of fraud losses; • fraud alert handling times; • root cause analysis of operational or process failures, gaps in onboarding or monitoring controls, and data quality issues; • key trends, including fraud typologies being exploited by criminals, customer vulnerability and customer behaviour; and • information from customers on the enabling tech and telecommunication platforms used in a fraud incident. Risk assessment 4.2.1D A thorough understanding of its financial crime risks is key if a firm is to apply proportionate and effective systems and controls. Firms should identify and assess the fraud risks to which it is exposed. We expect a firm to consider the full implications of the breadth of fraud risks it faces, which may have wider effects on its reputation, its customers and the markets in which it operates. FCG 2.2.4 sets out our expectations on business-wide risk assessments for financial crime. Examples of good practice Examples of poor practice • The firm takes a view on what areas of the firm are most vulnerable to fraudsters, and tailors defences accordingly. This could include fraud risks in products, services, delivery channels and customer journeys. • The firm fails to identify new or emerging fraud risks, limiting its ability to adapt systems and controls in response. • The firm considers the risk associated with various fraud types and typologies (eg, investment fraud as an APP fraud typology), when assessing the fraud risks. • The firm fails to consider fraud risks when new products and delivery channels are developed. • The firm can evidence the findings of risk assessments and evidence what actions were taken in response, to help protect customers from becoming the victim of fraud.

pages.text: FCA 202X/YY Page 23 of 67 Policies and procedures 4.2.1E FCG 2.2.5 sets out our expectation that a firm must have in place up-to-date policies and procedures appropriate to its business which should be readily accessible, effective and understood by all relevant staff. We expect these policies and procedures to include the firm’s arrangements for managing the potential harms arising from its fraud risks. Staff recruitment, vetting, training, awareness and remuneration 4.2.1F FCG 2.2.6 sets out our expectations in relation to recruitment, vetting, training, awareness and remuneration. In line with these expectations, firms should ensure that the staff they employ in fraud-specific roles possess the skills, knowledge and expertise to carry out their functions effectively. We expect all employees to receive regular fraud training to ensure staff at all levels are aware of the role they play in fraud prevention. Examples of good practice Examples of poor practice • Anti-fraud good practice is shared widely within the firm. • Employees do not receive appropriate training to equip them to identify suspicious behaviours in relation to fraud. • Employees in fraud-specific roles receive more specific and focused training. • Sales incentives act to encourage staff or management to turn a blind eye to potential fraud. • To guard against insider fraud, staff in high-risk positions (eg, the finance department or trading floor) are subject to enhanced vetting and closer scrutiny. ‘Four eyes’ procedures (see FCG Annex 1 for common terms) are in place. • Remuneration structures may incentivise behaviour that increases the risk of mortgage fraud. Customer treatment 4.2.1H We expect firms to have appropriate systems and controls in place to ensure they are engaging with customers appropriately in relation to fraud, including: • ensuring that customers have easily accessible routes for reporting instances of fraud, as well as suspicions of fraud; • ensuring they consider customer vulnerability; • ensuring that legal obligations in relation to reimbursement are met; • ensuring that appropriate support is provided to customers that have been victims of fraud; and • ensuring that customers have accessible routes for raising complaints in relation to fraud. These systems and controls should support the firms’ obligations under the Consumer Duty in relation to the standard of care they should be providing to customers. Examples of good practice Examples of poor practice • Teams are adequately resourced to respond to customer queries in relation to fraud, helping ensure they can take prompt action to prevent fraud and recover funds where appropriate. • Firms do not test their internal responses to fraud reports (or reports on suspicions of fraud), leading to slow or inadequate responses going unchecked. • The firm’s routes for reporting fraud (or suspicions of fraud) are easily accessible, consistent across all levels and types of customers, and responded to promptly. • Firms rely on passive anti-fraud messaging and content. • Firms engage with customers to raise awareness of fraud risks to help empower customers to better protect themselves from becoming victims of fraud. • Firms’ responses to complaints are insufficiently tailored to the specific case.

APP fraud and money mules 4.2.1I FCG 4.2.1I to FCG 4.2.1L set out our expectations for onboarding, monitoring and reporting, through the lens of tackling APP fraud and money mules. To support the general themes for fraud systems and controls (set out in FCG 4.2), firms should consider whether the guidance and good practice examples set out below can be also applied to other fraud types. APP fraud APP fraud is where a victim is deceived into authorising a payment either: • to an account that they think belongs to a legitimate payee but is actually controlled by a fraudster; or • for something they believed was legitimate but is actually fraudulent. APP fraud has significant financial consequences for victims and undermines security and trust in the UK economy. The FCA’s guidance on APP fraud aims to support the efforts across the wider system to tackle APP fraud, including: • Confirmation of Payee (CoP) – the name-checking service designed to reduce APP fraud and misdirected payments. Firms are required to implement API solutions to connect with Pay.UK’s central CoP directory. It covers 99% of Faster Payments and CHAPS transactions in the UK. • Payment Services Regulations 2017 – payment service providers (PSPs) can slow down the processing of outbound APP transactions where they have reasonable grounds to suspect fraud or dishonesty on the part of someone other than the payer. • APP scams reimbursement requirement – requires sending firms to reimburse in-scope APP scams reported by their customers, within 5 or (in exceptional circumstances) 35 business days, with limited exceptions. The sending firm can claim 50% of the cost of reimbursement from the receiving firm, with a maximum reimbursement limit of up to £85,000 per APP scam claim. The requirement applies for both Faster Payments and CHAPS transactions sent and received in the UK. APP fraud typologies There are various fraud typologies within APP fraud, including purchase scams, advanced fee fraud and romance fraud. Another key typology is investment fraud, which typically involves misappropriation of funds or fraud by deception, and which may be facilitated through opaque investment structures, unauthorised collective investment schemes or Ponzi schemes.

pages.text: FCA 202X/YY Page 26 of 67 We expect firms to consider the risks of different APP fraud typologies, including investment fraud, as part of their anti-fraud systems and controls. Money mules Money muling is a money-laundering technique where criminals use ‘money mule’ bank accounts to store and transfer criminal funds. A ‘money mule’ is recruited by criminals to move the criminal funds, either knowingly or unknowingly. Where an individual is an unknowingly involved money mule, they will often have been deceived by fraudsters, who present seemingly legitimate opportunities or plausible explanations to recruit individuals. Money mule networks play a significant role in both enabling fraud and facilitating the movement and cashing-out of the proceeds of fraud. Onboarding 4.2.1J FCG 3.2.4 sets out our expectations in relation to customer due diligence (CDD) checks. Firms must identify their customers and understand the purpose and intended nature of the customer’s relationship with the firm. Firms must collect information about the customer, which should be sufficient to obtain a complete picture of the risk associated with the business relationship and provide a meaningful basis for subsequent monitoring. We expect firms to take proactive steps to consider the types of checks that will help mitigate the fraud risks relevant to their customers, as well as the risks associated with receiving and moving the proceeds of fraud (money muling). Firms should consider the types of onboarding checks that will create a holistic view of the customer to provide a meaningful basis to support the firm’s approach to fraud risk management and subsequent fraud monitoring. Firms should take steps to update their understanding of the customer and any associated risks throughout the lifecycle of the customer relationship. Red flags for suspicious activity include, but are not limited to: • changes in behavioural biometrics that are not aligned to the firm’s understanding of the customer’s expected behaviour; • changes in expected turnover of account (eg, an increase in transactions or payment amounts); • negative Confirmation of Payee (CoP) results; • creation of new payees with high value transactions; • customers seeking funds from various sources (eg, loans, borrowing from friends or family, liquidating assets); • prompt dispersal of funds from a receiving account; • sudden changes in personal circumstances; and • customers using increasingly desperate tones in communications. A firm should consider its fraud risks when developing systems and controls to allow for risk-based monitoring across all complexity levels and ensure there is sufficient focus on both inbound and outbound transaction monitoring. These systems and controls should be kept under regular review to ensure they remain aligned to the firm’s fraud risks. Where alerts arise during monitoring, we expect firms to have adequate resource in place for fraud investigations to ensure the quality and speed of customer service is not negatively impacted. We also expect firms to keep comprehensive records of any subsequent investigations to ensure there is a clear evidential basis for objective decision making. Having effective monitoring systems and controls in place to swiftly detect unusual activity will assist a firm’s ability to deploy appropriate frictions to help prevent APP fraud. We expect firms to consider appropriate warnings for customers and deploy these at appropriate points throughout the payment journey, to help prevent customers falling victim to APP fraud. Ongoing monitoring is an important tool in detecting and disrupting money mule activity. We expect firms to have systems and controls in place to analyse the flow of funds, to help identify and disrupt mule activity originating from different fraud types, as well as help detect further account holders who may have received funds associated with mule activity, helping stop mule networks. Firms should consider which money mule indicators are relevant to their business and customer base. Money mule indicators include, but are not limited to: • unexpected or unexplained deposits into accounts; • changes in expected account turnover; • rapid dispersal of funds through networks of accounts (often within minutes of receipt); • movement of funds to international jurisdictions;

pages.text: FCA 202X/YY Page 34 of 67 4.2.1L As set out in FCG 3.2.10, firms must have a nominated officer who has a legal obligation to report any knowledge or suspicions of money laundering to the NCA through a suspicious activity report (SAR). Where firms know or suspect that fraudulent activity has resulted in money laundering, the nominated officer must report this through a SAR. Firms should also have policies and procedures in place for reporting instances of fraud to the relevant authorities, such as Report Fraud or relevant law enforcement agencies. Fraud databases play an important role in helping firms detect and prevent fraud. The value firms gain from using these databases, and the value they provide to the cross-system approach to tackling fraud, is contingent on engagement from industry participants in providing reliable and credible intel. Reporting on fraud data at an industry level plays a key role in tackling fraud across the whole system, where sharing a range of information can help firms develop improved mitigation tactics and help identify emerging fraud trends or risks. We encourage firms, where appropriate and subject to legal and regulatory requirements, to share key fraud information through public-sector or industry-led data sharing initiatives, act on information received and meaningfully contribute to any industry databases they use to support their systems and controls. This is separate from, and does not affect, firms’ SAR reporting obligations. APP fraud Examples of good practice Examples of poor practice • Firms analyse internal fraud data to identify key trends in APP fraud typologies and engage with cross-system initiatives for data sharing to assist other firms with their efforts to detect and prevent fraud. • The firm fails to act appropriately, and in a timely manner, following the receipt of specific intelligence or alert information from industry peers, law enforcement agency or other relevant authority in relation to APP fraud. • Firms which have suspicions about customers or accounts associated with APP fraud share relevant information with other firms promptly and efficiently, to assist efforts to investigate fraud claims. • The firm takes proactive steps to analyse information received from relevant data sharing initiatives to determine whether similar trends exist in its own

Investment fraud 4.2.5 UK consumers are targeted by share-sale frauds and other scams including land-banking frauds, unauthorised collective investment schemes and Ponzi schemes. Examples of good practice Examples of poor practice • A bank regularly assesses the risk to itself and its customers of losses from fraud, including investment fraud, in accordance with their established risk management framework. The risk assessment does not only cover situations where the bank could cover losses, but also where customers could lose and not be reimbursed by the bank. Resource allocation and mitigation measures are informed by this assessment. • A bank has performed no risk assessment that considers the risk to customers from investment fraud. • A bank contacts customers if it suspects a payment is being made to an investment fraudster. • A bank fails to use actionable, credible information it has about known or suspected perpetrators of investment fraud in its financial crime prevention systems. • A bank has transaction monitoring rules designed to detect specific types of investment fraud. pages.text: FCA 202X/YY Page 38 of 67 5.1 Introduction ... 5.1.2 Customers routinely entrust firms with important personal data; if this falls into criminal hands, fraudsters can attempt to undertake transactions in the customer’s name. Where that data is compromised, criminals may use it to facilitate fraud, including by impersonating customers or undertaking unauthorised transactions. Firms must take special care of their customers’ should protect personal data, and comply with the data protection principles set out in Schedule 1 to the obligations under the UK General Data Protection Regulation (UK GDPR) and the Data Protection Act 1998 2018. The Information Commissioner’s Office provides guidance on the Data Protection Act and the responsibilities it imposes on data controllers and processors. See section 4 and schedule 1 Data Protection Act 1998. Firms should have appropriate systems and controls to prevent, detect and respond to data security incidents that may increase the risk of financial crime. Guidance is available from the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO). 5.2 Themes Governance 5.2.1 ... Self-assessment questions: • How is responsibility for data security apportioned? • Does the firm’s assessment of data security and financial crime risk consider emerging technologies and digital assets, including vulnerabilities associated with digital asset activities, wallets, distributed ledger technology and third-party service providers? • Has the firm ever lost customer data? If so, what remedial actions did it take? Did it contact customers? Did it review its systems? • What management information (MI), dashboards or reporting does the firm use to identify, monitor and escalate data security incidents, unauthorised access, vulnerabilities, customer data exposures or breaches? Is MI provided in a sufficiently timely manner to support effective decision-making and remediation? • How does the firm monitor that suppliers of outsourced services treat customer data appropriately? • How does the firm obtain assurance that technology-enabled or automated financial crime controls operate effectively? Five Six fallacies of data loss and identity fraud 5.2.2 1. ‘The customer data we hold is too limited or too piecemeal to be of value to fraudsters.’ This is misconceived: skilled fraudsters can supplement a small core of data by accessing several different public sources and use impersonation to encourage victims to reveal more. Ultimately, they build up enough information to pose successfully as their victim. 2. ‘Only individuals with a high net worth are attractive targets for identity fraudsters.’ In fact, people of all ages, in all occupations and in all income groups are vulnerable if their data is lost. 3. ‘Only large firms with millions of customers are likely to be targeted.’ Wrong. Even a small firm’s customer database might be sold and re-sold for a substantial sum. 4. ‘The threat to data security is only external.’ This is not always the case. Insiders have more opportunity to steal customer data and may do so either to commit fraud themselves, or to pass it on to organised criminals 5. ‘No customer has ever notified us that their identity has been stolen, so our firm must be impervious to data breaches.’ The truth may be closer to the opposite: firms that successfully detect data loss do so because they have effective risk-management systems. Firms with weak controls or monitoring are likely to be oblivious to any loss. Furthermore, when fraud does occur, a victim rarely has the means to identify where their data was lost because data is held in so many places. ‘Partial, historical or seemingly insignificant customer data cannot be valuable to fraudsters.’ Information from multiple sources may be combined to facilitate identity fraud or social engineering attacks. Firms should apply appropriate protections to all customer data, not only complete or current records. 6. ‘Digital identification is foolproof.’ Digital identification and verification tools can improve security but are not immune from abuse. Firms should consider emerging threats such as deepfakes, synthetic identities and AI-enabled spoofing, and regularly review whether their controls remain effective. Controls 5.2.3 ...

See https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/financial-sanctions-faqs. The Office of Trade Sanctions Implementation (OTSI) within the Department for Business and Trade helps to ensure implementation and enforcement of trade sanctions in the United Kingdom. OTSI provides guidance to assist firms in understanding and complying with trade sanctions regulations. If firms become aware of a breach of UK trade sanctions, they must notify OTSI in accordance with the relevant provisions. Firms should report to HMRC if the suspected breach relates to breaches of export controls and trade sanctions involving UK customs. See government guidance for reporting suspected breaches of trade sanctions. Firms should also consider whether they should report sanctions breaches to the FCA. SUP 15.3 contains general notification requirements. Firms are required to tell us, for example, about significant rule breaches (see SUP 15.3.11R(1)). Firms should therefore consider whether a sanctions breach is the result of any matter within the scope of SUP 15.3 – for example, a significant failure in their financial crime systems and controls. 7.1.6 Alongside financial sanctions, the government imposes controls on certain types of trade. As part of this, the export of goods and services for use in nuclear, radiological, chemical or biological weapons programmes is subject to strict controls. Proliferators seek to gain access to this technology illegally: aiding them is an offence under the Anti-Terrorism, Crime and Security Act 2001. Note that the Treasury can also use powers under the Counter Terrorism Act 2008 (see FCG Annex 1) to direct financial firms to, say, cease business with certain customers involved in proliferation activity. pages.text: FCA 202X/YY Page 46 of 67 Governance 7.2A.2 The guidance in FCG 2.2.1 on governance in relation to financial crime also applies to sanctions. We expect senior management to take clear responsibility for managing sanctions risks, which should be treated in the same manner as other risks faced by the business. There should be evidence that senior management are actively engaged in the firm’s approach to addressing the risks of non-compliance with UK sanctions. Where they identify gaps, they should remediate them. Self-assessment questions: • Has the firm clearly allocated responsibility for adherence to the sanctions regime? To whom? • How does the firm monitor performance? (For example, statistical or narrative reports on matches or breaches.) • How are senior management kept up to date with sanctions compliance issues? • Does the firm’s organisational structure with respect to sanctions compliance across different jurisdictions promote a coordinated approach and accountability? • Does the firm have evidence that sanctions issues are escalated where warranted? • Where sanctions controls processes rely on resource external to the firm, is there appropriate oversight and understanding of that resource? Examples of good practice Examples of poor practice • An individual of sufficient authority is responsible for overseeing the firm’s adherence to UK sanctions. • The firm believes payments to sanctioned individuals and entities are permitted when the sums are small. Without a licence from the OFSI, this could be a criminal offence. • Sanctions compliance is embedded within the wider financial crime control framework. The relevance of wider controls is considered, including adverse media screening, blockchain analysis and transaction monitoring for unusual trading patterns. • Multinational firms lack the communication between global and regional sanctions teams necessary to manage compliance with UK sanctions laws, regulations and guidance.

pages.text: FCA 202X/YY Page 52 of 67 Where there are restrictions in relation to specified financial and investment activities, such as in dealing in certain transferable securities or money market instruments, sanctions screening may also involve screening for those activities. A firm should have effective, up-to-date screening systems appropriate to the nature, size and risk of its business. Although screening itself is not a legal requirement, screening new customers, counterparties to transactions and payments against the UK Sanctions List, and screening existing customers when any amendments are made to the list, helps to ensure that firms will not breach UK sanctions. Screening polices 7.2A.7 Self-assessment questions: • If a customer was referred to your firm, how does the firm ensure the person is not designated? (Does the firm screen the customer against the list itself, or does it seek assurances from the referring party?) • Does your firm have a clear policy on which customers, counterparties and payments are subject to screening, and what related data is subject to screening? This may also include policies for screening related parties, including directors and ultimate beneficial owners. • Does your firm have a clear policy on what sanctions regimes it is seeking to screen against, and with what frequency? • If using an outsourced service, does your firm have appropriate control and oversight of its sanctions screening controls? • Has your firm documented its consideration of other forms of screening beyond name screening, such as for high-risk jurisdictions or services and goods? Examples of good practice Examples of poor practice • It is clear at what stage customers are screened in different situations (eg, when customers are passed from agents or other companies in the group). • A firm assumes that an intermediary has screened a customer, but does not check this. • Where exposure to trade sanctions risk is identified, the firm considers screening for restricted goods and services, high-risk ports and countries, and sanctioned vessels as well as designated persons. • A firm uses manual screening processes; however, the increasing size of its business has not been considered in its sanctions screening processes.

Asset freezing and licences 7.2A.12 When a financial sanction is an asset freeze, the funds and economic resources belonging to or owned, held or controlled by a designated person are generally to be frozen immediately by the person in possession or control of them, unless there is an exception in the legislation they can rely on, or they have a licence from OFSI. In addition to asset freezes, OFSI may issue licences for other sanctions measures, including sectoral sanctions and ancillary services bans. Relevant firms are required to report to OFSI, as soon as practicable, the nature and amount or quantity of any funds or economic resources they hold for a customer who is a designated person. Additionally, firms are required to report all frozen assets held for designated persons to OFSI annually, including details of all the funds or economic resources frozen in the UK as well as those overseas where the funds or economic resources are subject to UK financial sanctions legislation. For more information, see OFSI’s guidance on reporting. Self-assessment questions: • Does your firm have clear policies and procedures as to when funds and economic resources are frozen or released? • Have you assessed how any frozen funds and economic resources in your firm’s possession or control are maintained in compliance with UK sanctions? • Does your firm have clear policies and procedures to assess, utilise and monitor the use of OFSI licences and statutory exceptions? Reporting and assessing potential sanctions breaches 7.2A.13 Relevant firms are required to report to OFSI where they know, or have reasonable cause to suspect, a breach of financial sanctions, and notify OFSI if: • a person they are dealing with, directly or indirectly, is a designated person; • they hold any frozen assets; or • they discover or suspect any breach while conducting their business. Relevant firms are required to report to OTSI where they know or have reasonable cause to suspect a breach of trade sanctions and should additionally report to HMRC if the suspected breach relates to breaches of export controls and trade sanctions involving UK customs. In line with Principle 11, SUP 15.3.8G(2), SUP 15.3.11R(1) and FCG 7, firms must consider whether they need to notify us – for example, whether potential breaches of sanctions resulted from a significant failure in its systems and controls. Additionally, if there are suspicions of money laundering or terrorist financing as a result of sanctions breaches, firms should consider their obligations to submit a Suspicious Activity Report to the UK Financial Intelligence Unit (UKFIU). Firms are required to tell us about significant rule breaches (see SUP 15.3.11R(1)), or a significant failure in their financial crime systems and controls. • A firm has poorly defined escalation and reporting procedures to identify to which authority to report. • Significant deficiencies in the firm’s systems and controls resulting in potential sanctions breaches are reported to the FCA. Proliferation finance 7.2A.14 Alongside financial and trade sanctions, the government imposes controls on certain types of trade in order to achieve foreign policy objectives. The export of goods and services for use in nuclear, radiological, chemical or biological weapons programmes is subject to strict controls. Firms’ systems and controls and policies and procedures should address and mitigate the proliferation risks they face. Firms are also required to carry out proliferation financing risk assessments under regulation 18A of the Money Laundering Regulations, either as part of the existing practice-wide risk assessment or as a standalone document. Proliferation financing may utilise mechanisms similar to those used in sanctions evasion, and some proliferation finance measures are implemented through the use of targeted financial sanctions (including asset freezes). As a result, earlier sections of FCG 7 on sanctions risks are also relevant, including in relation to customer due diligence, risk assessments, screening, transaction monitoring and evasion detection. Self-assessment questions: • Does your firm finance trade with high-risk countries? If so, is enhanced due diligence carried out on counterparties and goods? Where doubt remains, is evidence sought from exporters that the trade is legitimate?

Case study – deficient sanctions systems and controls 7.2A.15 In October 2024, the FCA fined Starling Bank Limited £29m for financial crime failings related to its financial sanctions screening framework. • In January 2023, Starling identified that, since the implementation of its financial sanctions screening framework in 2017, its automated screening system had only been screening the names of new and existing customers against individuals on the Sanctions List with UK citizenship or UK residency. • A subsequent review of Starling’s financial sanctions framework identified wider systemic weaknesses, including deficiencies in its financial sanctions risk assessment, policies and procedures, the testing and calibration of screening systems, and a lack of effective management information on alert volumes and trends. • In addition, Starling breached a voluntary requirement (VREQ) restricting it from opening new accounts for high-risk customers, opening over 54,000 accounts for 49,000 high-risk customers between September 2021 and November 2023. Due to the breaches of the VREQ and Principle 3 of the FCA’s Principles for Businesses, the FCA imposed a financial penalty of £29m on Starling Bank Limited.
