3 Chapter 1Summary1.1 Financial crime is becoming more sophisticated and complex. We’re consulting on changes to our Financial Crime Guide (the Guide) to help firms assess and strengthen their financial crime systems and controls. 1.2 Financial crime causes wide-ranging harm: it damages lives and livelihoods, enables serious and organised crime, undermines trust in the financial system and weakens the wider economy. Tackling it is one of our priorities and requires a coordinated effort across industry, government, law enforcement and regulators. Firms are essential partners in that collective effort. Their work to detect, prevent and disrupt financial crime helps protect consumers and safeguard the integrity of the financial system. 1.3 The updates we propose are informed by insights from our supervision and wider developments. We want the Guide to continue to help firms understand our expectations, strengthen their financial crime systems and controls and support their efforts to detect, prevent and disrupt financial crime. 1.4 The Guide includes self-assessment questions and examples of good and poor practice drawn from our supervisory work and wider financial crime publications.1.5 The Guide does not contain rules nor impose any new requirements. We expect firms to have read and considered it, using it as well as their own their judgement to establish effective policies and controls.1.6 Firms should factor in the UK’s System Priorities to demonstrate how they counter financial crime risk. The System Priorities framework is developing with focus on delivering more through Public Private Partnership.1.7 For further information on how these changes aim to prevent harm and how the consultation aligns with FCA objectives, see paragraph 1.13 and Chapter 2.1.8 This CP should be read by:• all FCA financial crime supervised firms, including firms we supervise under The Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds (Information on the Payer) Regulations 2017 (MLRs), such as Annex I Financial Institutions and cryptoasset businesses.1.9 The CP may also be of interest to:• individuals and organisations working with firms subject to our financial crime and MLRs supervision• financial services trade organisations and professional bodies• any other parties interested in our financial crime supervision, such as non-governmental organisations working on financial crime prevention, or academics

4What we want to update1.10 We want the Guide to be clear, reflect our recent findings, and help firms identify and assess the right financial crime controls.1 .11 We propose changes to the following areas:Fraud: Updates to reflect supervisory expectations and lessons from our multi-firm work on authorised push payment (APP) fraud and money mules, responding to industry feedback for more guidance. Cryptoassets: From 25 October 2027, firms carrying out certain cryptoasset activities in the UK will need to be authorised by us under the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (Cryptoassets) Regulations 2026. The Guide will help firms meet our expectations when developing and maintaining financial crime systems and controls. Financial and trade sanctions: The UK’s sanctions regime has evolved since the Guide was last updated, and since the Office of Trade Sanctions Implementation (OTSI) was established. We propose to update this section to reflect these developments and include examples of good and poor practice drawn from our supervisory work.Proliferation financing: Supervisory work has highlighted the need for enhanced guidance on proliferation financing risks and controls, including further detail on our expectations for firms.Data security: We want the guidance to keep pace with today’s financial crime and cyber risks, data protection legislation, governance and crisis communication, and emerging risks associated with AI, synthetic identity fraud and digital assets.Financial crime system and controls: Clarifying our expectations for firms using Banking as a Service (BaaS) delivery models, including where services are outsourced, white labelled or provided through embedded finance partnerships.Money laundering and terrorist financing: Updates so that the Guide remains current and reflects developments in industry practice, such as electronic verification, third party tools and outsourcing arrangements, and clarifying the importance of co-operation and information sharing. Consequential changes: Updates to the Guide, including reflecting recent changes to the MLRs that came into force in June 2026, updating expired links and references (including references to European Union legislation), and refreshing case studies.1.12 Further details are in Chapters 2-3 and Appendix 1.

5 Intended outcomes1.13 The proposed changes are to help firms:• reduce financial crime: We want to make sure that firms and markets are not used for financial crime. These changes give firms guidance on how they might evaluate or set up their systems and controls.• maintain confidence in the financial system: Confidence in the UK financial system depends on firms preventing harm to the public. We have proposed changes so that the Guide continues to reflect our expectations, and protects confidence in and the integrity of the financial system.• protect consumers: Effective financial crime systems and controls protect consumers from harm. The proposed changes reinforce our expectations that firms maintain controls that are proportionate to the risks they face.Outcomes and measuring success1.14 We will evaluate the impact of the consultation by analysing engagement and feedback on the proposed changes.1.15 We will continue to update the guidance in line with our supervisory findings and publications. We also welcome feedback on chapters from stakeholders on chapters or areas not addressed in this CP that they consider we should focus on in future.Next steps1.16 We welcome your feedback on our proposed guidance in Appendix 1 by 24 December 2026.The specific questions for feedback are in Annex 1.1 .17 You can submit your responses via the form on our website. If you are not able to use the form, write to us at C P 26 -3 8 @fca.org.uk. 1.18 We will consider your comments and publish feedback on this CP, along with the final amended text of the Guide, in a Policy Statement. Your feedback will also instruct our future updates to the Guide.

6Chapter 2Proposed changes Fraud2.1 Fraud has significant financial and emotional consequences for victims. It also undermines security and trust in the UK financial system. In recent years, government, law enforcement, regulators and industry have stepped up efforts to tackle it. 2.2 We have assessed systems and controls for detecting and preventing authorised push payment (APP) fraud and money mule activity at Payment Service Providers (PSPs), including retail banks, and payments and e-money firms. We have heard repeated calls from industry for more guidance on fraud.2.3 So we propose making updates to Chapter 4 – Fraud. These will incorporate the findings of systems and controls publications, including:• Anti-fraud controls and complaint handing in firms (with a focus on APP fraud)• Proceeds of fraud – detecting and preventing money mules • Firms’ use of the National Fraud Database (NFD) and money mule account detection tools• Combating romance fraud – prevention, detection and supporting victimsOur updated guidance focuses on APP fraud and money mule systems and controls, to help the firms we regulate meet their financial crime obligations. The new section on APP fraud and money mules is structured around three areas: onboarding, monitoring and reporting. The updated guidance is focussed on APP fraud as the overarching typology and does not reference specific fraud types associated with APP fraud. To reflect this, we have incorporated the guidance on investment fraud into the updated APP fraud section and set out that firms should be considering the risks associated with different APP fraud typologies as part of its anti-fraud systems and controls. We remain committed to tackling investment fraud:• we have introduced the Firm Checker tool for consumers to check firms are authorised by us and have the permissions to provide the services they want before making investments• we publish the FCA warning list of unauthorised firms• we publish information to help consumers protect themselves from scams • we have led international action to stop illegal influencers putting consumers’ money at risk.

7 Onboarding • We expect firms to consider the onboarding checks that will help mitigate both the risks of fraud and of moving the proceeds of fraud.• We have shared examples of good and poor practice for onboarding. They include: –Good practice: where firms have built a holistic view of the customer, reviewed a range of sources to aid behavioural profiling, used fraud databases, identified customer vulnerability, and implemented checks to identify synthetic or counterfeit documentation. –Poor practice: failing to keep accurate records of onboarding checks, completing basic checks that do not inform a holistic picture of the customer, and only being aware of customer vulnerabilities after a fraud has occurred.Monitoring• Swift and proactive detection of unusual activity helps firms spot weaknesses in systems and controls that fraudsters might exploit. • We have included some potential APP fraud indicators, such as changes in behavioural biometrics, changes in expected account turnover, negative Confirmation of Payee (COP) results, creation of new payees with high value transactions, and customers using increasingly desperate tones in communications. • We have included some money mule activity indicators, such as including unexpected or unexplained deposits, rapid dispersal of funds, changes in dormant accounts, online banking credentials changing, and changes to device or contact details are inconsistent with the firm’s knowledge of the customer. • There are examples of good and poor practice for APP fraud and money mule monitoring. They include: –Good practice: monitoring inbound and outbound transactions, reviewing and testing transaction monitoring alerts, customer warnings, prompt investigation of money mule alerts, and policies and procedures for the firm’s response to money mules. –Poor practice: inadequate staff training to identify APP fraud or money mule indicators, lack of feedback loops on updates to systems and controls, a focus on outbound transaction monitoring only, failing to promptly implement new transaction monitoring alerts, and failing to review or assess the impact of customer warnings. Reporting • We expect firms to have policies and procedures for reporting instances of fraud to the authorities. Reporting on fraud data, as well as wider information sharing, at an industry level plays a key role in tackling fraud across the whole system. We encourage firms to contribute to data sharing initiatives, in support of the wider cross-system approach for tackling fraud. • There are examples of good and poor practice for APP fraud and money mule reporting. They include:

8 –Good practice: identifying APP fraud trends and sharing them through cross-system initiatives for data sharing, sharing key information promptly and efficiently, assessing money mule cases individually, and promptly reporting relevant cases to industry databases. –Poor practice: failing to act after receiving specific intelligence, and failing to keep comprehensive records in relation to decisions to file (or not to file) to fraud databases. 2.4 In addition, we propose to build on existing fraud guidance by strengthening content relating to fraud risk assessments, governance and oversight, and using management information and assurance to identify, monitor and escalate risks.2.5 We propose to include examples of how firms may respond to evolving fraud typologies, through staff training, analytical tools and fraud prevention controls.2.6 These updates complement and are consistent with the UK’s wider fraud policy and strategy. This covers: APP scams reimbursement requirements, the Payment Services (Amendment) Regulations 2024 (slowing down outbound payment processing where there are reasonable grounds to suspect fraud), system prioritisation to tackle the biggest economic threats under Economic Crime Plan 2 (ECP2), and the UK Fraud Strategy 2026-2029.Question 1: At the time of publication, investment fraud was increasing: UK Finance data showed a 26% rise in cases and a 40% increase in losses between 2024 and 2025. Are there particular challenges in detecting and preventing investment fraud through systems and controls? What guidance on systems and controls for investment fraud should be included alongside the broader APP fraud guidance?Cryptoassets 2.7 Since January 2020, cryptoasset businesses operating in the UK, defined in the MLRs as cryptoasset exchange providers or custodian wallet providers, have been required to register with the FCA. Following the Financial Services and Markets Act (Cryptoasset) Regulations 2026 (Cryptoasset Regulations), from 25 October 2027, firms carrying out certain regulated cryptoasset activities by way of business in the UK will need to be authorised by us and comply with our financial crime rules (as published in PS26/13). 2.8 Firms in scope of the Cryptoasset Regulations will still need to comply with their obligations under the MLRs, as well as other financial crime legislation such as the Terrorism Act 2000 and Proceeds of Crime Act 2002.2.9 Many firms will be new to these regulations, and we want our guidance to help them understand and be aware of compliance with financial crime expectations under

9 Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 and the MLRs. Our proposed updates will give examples of good and poor practice, helping firms implement systems and controls to prepare for applications.2.10 The 2025 National Risk Assessment ranked the risk for money laundering as ‘high’ and for terrorist financing as ‘medium’ for cryptoassets. The cross-border and fast-moving nature of blockchain and cryptoasset transactions make detection and enforcement uniquely difficult. Our proposed updates to the Guide clarify our expectations that firms adopt a risk-based approach to identifying and mitigating these risks.2 .11 Our proposed guidance includes:• Good and poor practice examples on the triggers for enhanced due diligence, reflecting the financial crime risks faced by firms engaging with cryptoassets. • Good and poor practice examples of how firms meet our expectations on systems and controls, such as for onboarding and monitoring, and the use of blockchain analytics for firms engaging in cryptoasset activities.• Further guidance on firms’ obligations for complying with the Travel Rule.2.12 We are reminding firms of our expectations on governance. We expect all firms, including start-ups, to proactively monitor and adapt their approach as their business grows and matures.2.13 In addition, we are proposing to add a self-assessment question to help firms consider whether their policies, procedures and staff training adequately distinguish between obligations under the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002 and the Terrorism Act 2000. Financial sanctions and trade sanctions2.14 All firms should understand how their business may be exposed to sanctions risk and ensure their controls are proportionate to that exposure. Our supervisory work has shown that they’d benefit from more guidance on assessing their exposure and testing their controls.2.15 We are proposing updates to Chapter 7 of the Guide to set out our expectations and examples of good and poor practice. In particular, we propose to cover trade alongside financial sanctions, reflecting developments in the UK’s sanctions framework including the establishment of OTSI.2.16 The updates are to help firms consider their exposure to risk from their customers, counterparties, intermediaries, jurisdictions, goods, services, transactions, payments and payment messages. The guidance will help them assess their risk assessments, customer due diligence (CDD), screening, monitoring and reporting.

102 .17 We propose to update references to relevant authorities. The revised chapter will refer to OFSI for financial sanctions, OTSI for trade sanctions, HMRC where suspected breaches relate to export controls or customs matters, and to us where issues may indicate weaknesses in a firm’s financial crime systems and controls.2.18 The revised chapter will improve guidance on governance, management information, risk assessment, CDD, screening, evasion detection, asset freezing, licensing and breach reporting. It will reorganise some existing material so that the chapter is easier to follow and refreshed with more recent FCA enforcement examples.2.19 The specific guidance includes:• Explaining how firms may be exposed to financial and trade sanctions risk through their business relationships, activities and transaction flows.• Clarifying the respective roles of OFSI, OTSI, HMRC and the FCA, including the circumstances in which matters may need to be reported to each authority.• Strengthening guidance on governance and management information, including senior management oversight, escalation, training and the monitoring of sanctions controls.• Expanding risk assessment guidance to address matters such as sanctions circumvention, intermediary countries and sectoral and trade sanctions.• Enhancing guidance on CDD and KYC, including the consideration of ownership structures, connected parties, counterparties and relevant trade information.• Reorganising the screening material to distinguish more clearly between screening policies, sanctions-list management, system calibration, testing and alert management.• Clarifying firms’ responsibilities when using third-party screening tools or outsourced arrangements, including oversight of vendor-configured settings and the timely, complete and accurate implementation of sanctions-list data.• Encouraging firms to consider monitoring beyond name screening, including risks associated with goods, vessels, ports, services and jurisdictions.• Developing guidance on detecting sanctions evasion through appropriate typologies, data analysis, thematic review and transaction monitoring.• Setting out practices for managing screening alerts, including resourcing, backlogs, internal decision-making standards and audit trails.• Updating guidance on asset freezing, licensing and suspected breaches, including escalation, root cause analysis and reporting to the relevant authorities.

11 Proliferation financing 2.20 We propose to update the proliferation financing material in Chapter 7. The revisions recognise that proliferation financing may involve mechanisms similar to sanctions evasion and clarifies how firms might manage the risk through existing controls.2.21 We propose to add self-assessment questions and examples of good and poor practice covering strategic export controls, dual-use and military goods, reporting and escalation procedures, the integration of proliferation financing into risk assessments, and how firms respond to published typologies when assessing their exposure to proliferation financing risks.2.22 It includes: • explaining how sanctions controls may help manage proliferation financing risk• guidance on higher-risk goods and activities, including strategic export controls, dual-use goods and military goods • guidance on documented reporting and escalation procedures for suspected proliferation financing breaches• updated good practice examples such as integrating proliferation financing risk into risk assessments, reviewing exposure after typology publications, and avoiding failures to incorporate PF risk into onboarding, CDD, screening and transaction monitoring. We also included examples of poor practice 2.23 In addition, if a new Proliferation Finance National Risk Assessment is published before we have finalised the Guide, we’ll include a reference to it. Data security2.24 We propose to update the Data Security guidance, so it reflects today’s financial crime and cyber risk landscape. Changes include:• updating outdated legislative references to align with the Data Protection Act 2018 and UK GDPR• strengthening governance expectations by incorporating board involvement, improved crisis communication; and• refreshing self-assessment material covering AI, synthetic identity fraud and digital asset-related risk 2.25 This will help firms assess whether their systems and controls are effective. The case studies and the ‘five fallacies of data loss and identify fraud’ section will be refreshed to reflect modern threats, including deepfakes. We’ll include learnings from recent enforcement cases, so that firms can benchmark themselves against risks.

12Financial crime systems and controls2.26 We propose to set out how financial crime obligations apply in Banking as a Service (BaaS) and embedded finance arrangements, both where the BaaS user is another regulated firm and where it is unregulated. The guidance reinforces that regulated firms are accountable for maintaining effective systems and controls across the delivery chain, including where activities are outsourced, white-labelled or delivered through embedded finance models.Money laundering and terrorist financing 2.27 Firms are increasingly using AI and other third-party tools in their financial crime systems and controls. They must apply governance and oversight to these and remain accountable for managing the financial crime risks they present. The tools must be proportionate to the firm’s risk profile and risk appetite, and subject to testing and validation. 2.28 We are proposing additions to the Guide so that it remains current and aligned with industry practice, such as expanded guidance on electronic verification. We have added examples of good and poor practice relating to notification obligations for PSPs and Intermediary Service Providers where there are repeated failures to comply with fund transfer requirements involving electronic transmission. We have also updated related terminology, including replacing references to Production Orders with Investigative Court Orders. 2.29 The banking and financial sector is critical national infrastructure, relied upon by businesses and the public every day. We have a duty to promote the resilience of the sector and its ability to withstand attempts to disrupt or deny services. We work closely with law enforcement agencies, regulators and other authorities to support stable, resilient and robust financial systems, maintained by effective co-operation and information sharing. We therefore propose to reinforce the importance of this between firms, regulators, law enforcement agencies and other relevant authorities.Consequential changes 2.30 We are proposing other changes to keep the Guide up to date, as a consequence of wider changes. These are:• Updating it to reflect amendments to the MLRs introduced in June 2026.• Removing references to European Union rules and supervisory authorities to keep it consistent with changes following the UK’s exit from the EU.• Refreshing links and more recent examples of outcomes on financial crime.• Including more links to useful material for firms to consult when conducting or reviewing their systems and controls.• Making other minor drafting changes.

16Annex 2Cost benefit analysisIntroduction1. The Financial Services and Markets Act (2000) require us to publish a cost benefit analysis (CBA) of our proposed rules. Specifically, section 138I requires us to publish a CBA of proposed rules, defined as ‘an analysis of the costs, together with an analysis of the benefits that will arise if the proposed rules are made’. 2. However, FSMA does not require us to produce and publish a CBA when proposing guidance (see section 139A of FSMA on power of the FCA to give guidance and section 139B of FSMA on the meaning of general guidance). As set out in our Statement of Policy on CBAs we may produce a CBA for general guidance if a high-level assessment of the impact of the proposal identifies an element of novelty, which may be in effect prescriptive or prohibitive, that may result in significant costs being incurred.3. Our Statement of Policy on CBAs provides that a CBA is undertaken where changes to guidance are likely to result in significant costs. In this case, we do not consider that significant costs will arise. The proposed updates reflect existing regulatory expectations and established industry practice and are intended to clarify and update existing guidance, not introduce new requirements. We therefore do not expect the proposals to result in a material increase in the frequency of, or time spent on, compliance activities, nor do we expect them to result in material costs to consumers, materially alter the products and services provided by firms, or have a material impact on competition or the wider economy.4. The proposals in this consultation relate to general guidance as defined in section 139B of FSMA. As explained in FCG 1.1.7, the Guide contains general guidance that is not binding and a firm’s departure from that guidance does not, of itself, indicate a breach of FCA rules. Therefore, we have not undertaken a CBA.

APP fraud and money mules 4.2.1I FCG 4.2.1I to FCG 4.2.1L set out our expectations for onboarding, monitoring and reporting, through the lens of tackling APP fraud and money mules. To support the general themes for fraud systems and controls (set out in FCG 4.2), firms should consider whether the guidance and good practice examples set out below can be also applied to other fraud types. APP fraud APP fraud is where a victim is deceived into authorising a payment either: • to an account that they think belongs to a legitimate payee but is actually controlled by a fraudster; or • for something they believed was legitimate but is actually fraudulent. APP fraud has significant financial consequences for victims and undermines security and trust in the UK economy. The FCA’s guidance on APP fraud aims to support the efforts across the wider system to tackle APP fraud, including: • Confirmation of Payee (CoP) – the name-checking service designed to reduce APP fraud and misdirected payments. Firms are required to implement API solutions to connect with Pay.UK’s central CoP directory. It covers 99% of Faster Payments and CHAPS transactions in the UK. • Payment Services Regulations 2017 – payment service providers (PSPs) can slow down the processing of outbound APP transactions where they have reasonable grounds to suspect fraud or dishonesty on the part of someone other than the payer. • APP scams reimbursement requirement – requires sending firms to reimburse in-scope APP scams reported by their customers, within 5 or (in exceptional circumstances) 35 business days, with limited exceptions. The sending firm can claim 50% of the cost of reimbursement from the receiving firm, with a maximum reimbursement limit of up to £85,000 per APP scam claim. The requirement applies for both Faster Payments and CHAPS transactions sent and received in the UK. APP fraud typologies There are various fraud typologies within APP fraud, including purchase scams, advanced fee fraud and romance fraud. Another key typology is investment fraud, which typically involves misappropriation of funds or fraud by deception, and which may be facilitated through opaque investment structures, unauthorised collective investment schemes or Ponzi schemes.

FCA 202X/YY Page 26 of 67 We expect firms to consider the risks of different APP fraud typologies, including investment fraud, as part of their anti-fraud systems and controls. Money mules Money muling is a money-laundering technique where criminals use ‘money mule’ bank accounts to store and transfer criminal funds. A ‘money mule’ is recruited by criminals to move the criminal funds, either knowingly or unknowingly. Where an individual is an unknowingly involved money mule, they will often have been deceived by fraudsters, who present seemingly legitimate opportunities or plausible explanations to recruit individuals. Money mule networks play a significant role in both enabling fraud and facilitating the movement and cashing-out of the proceeds of fraud. Onboarding 4.2.1J FCG 3.2.4 sets out our expectations in relation to customer due diligence (CDD) checks. Firms must identify their customers and understand the purpose and intended nature of the customer’s relationship with the firm. Firms must collect information about the customer, which should be sufficient to obtain a complete picture of the risk associated with the business relationship and provide a meaningful basis for subsequent monitoring. We expect firms to take proactive steps to consider the types of checks that will help mitigate the fraud risks relevant to their customers, as well as the risks associated with receiving and moving the proceeds of fraud (money muling). Firms should consider the types of onboarding checks that will create a holistic view of the customer to provide a meaningful basis to support the firm’s approach to fraud risk management and subsequent fraud monitoring. Firms should take steps to update their understanding of the customer and any associated risks throughout the lifecycle of the customer relationship. Monitoring 4.2.1K FCG 3.2.5 sets out that a firm must conduct ongoing monitoring of its business relationships on a risk-sensitive basis. This means scrutinising transactions and behaviour to ensure that they are consistent with what the firm knows about the customer. Swift and proactive detection of unusual activity helps firms identify weaknesses in controls for detecting and preventing fraud and identifying money mule activity, as well as helping to identify emerging patterns in customer or fraudster behaviour, before they can be more widely exploited. A firm should determine what represents suspicious activity for APP fraud, and relevant APP fraud typologies, based on the risks associated with its

FCA 202X/YY Page 29 of 67 business and customer base. Red flags for suspicious activity include, but are not limited to: • changes in behavioural biometrics that are not aligned to the firm’s understanding of the customer’s expected behaviour; • changes in expected turnover of account (eg, an increase in transactions or payment amounts); • negative Confirmation of Payee (CoP) results; • creation of new payees with high value transactions; • customers seeking funds from various sources (eg, loans, borrowing from friends or family, liquidating assets); • prompt dispersal of funds from a receiving account; • sudden changes in personal circumstances; and • customers using increasingly desperate tones in communications. A firm should consider its fraud risks when developing systems and controls to allow for risk-based monitoring across all complexity levels and ensure there is sufficient focus on both inbound and outbound transaction monitoring. These systems and controls should be kept under regular review to ensure they remain aligned to the firm’s fraud risks. Where alerts arise during monitoring, we expect firms to have adequate resource in place for fraud investigations to ensure the quality and speed of customer service is not negatively impacted. We also expect firms to keep comprehensive records of any subsequent investigations to ensure there is a clear evidential basis for objective decision making. Having effective monitoring systems and controls in place to swiftly detect unusual activity will assist a firm’s ability to deploy appropriate frictions to help prevent APP fraud. We expect firms to consider appropriate warnings for customers and deploy these at appropriate points throughout the payment journey, to help prevent customers falling victim to APP fraud. Ongoing monitoring is an important tool in detecting and disrupting money mule activity. We expect firms to have systems and controls in place to analyse the flow of funds, to help identify and disrupt mule activity originating from different fraud types, as well as help detect further account holders who may have received funds associated with mule activity, helping stop mule networks. Firms should consider which money mule indicators are relevant to their business and customer base. Money mule indicators include, but are not limited to: • unexpected or unexplained deposits into accounts; • changes in expected account turnover; • rapid dispersal of funds through networks of accounts (often within minutes of receipt); • movement of funds to international jurisdictions;

Five Six fallacies of data loss and identity fraud 5.2.2 1. ‘The customer data we hold is too limited or too piecemeal to be of value to fraudsters.’ This is misconceived: skilled fraudsters can supplement a small core of data by accessing several different public sources and use impersonation to encourage victims to reveal more. Ultimately, they build up enough information to pose successfully as their victim. 2. ‘Only individuals with a high net worth are attractive targets for identity fraudsters.’ In fact, people of all ages, in all occupations and in all income groups are vulnerable if their data is lost. 3. ‘Only large firms with millions of customers are likely to be targeted.’ Wrong. Even a small firm’s customer database might be sold and re-sold for a substantial sum. 4. ‘The threat to data security is only external.’ This is not always the case. Insiders have more opportunity to steal customer data and may do so either to commit fraud themselves, or to pass it on to organised criminals 5. ‘No customer has ever notified us that their identity has been stolen, so our firm must be impervious to data breaches.’ The truth may be closer to the opposite: firms that successfully detect data loss do so because they have effective risk-management systems. Firms with weak controls or monitoring are likely to be oblivious to any loss. Furthermore, when fraud does occur, a victim rarely has the means to identify where their data was lost because data is held in so many places. ‘Partial, historical or seemingly insignificant customer data cannot be valuable to fraudsters.’ Information from multiple sources may be combined to facilitate identity fraud or social engineering attacks. Firms should apply appropriate protections to all customer data, not only complete or current records. 6. ‘Digital identification is foolproof.’ Digital identification and verification tools can improve security but are not immune from abuse. Firms should consider emerging threats such as deepfakes, synthetic identities and AI-enabled spoofing, and regularly review whether their controls remain effective. Controls 5.2.3 ...

Screening customers, counterparties and payments 7.2A.6 Sanctions screening is the process of checking customer, counterparty and transactional data against the relevant sanctions lists to identify potential matches to sanctioned individuals, entities, jurisdictions, goods and services. Compliance with sanctions includes screening names and transactions, applying fuzzy-matching logic to detect variations, and generating alerts of potential sanctions matches for investigation.

FCA 202X/YY Page 52 of 67 Where there are restrictions in relation to specified financial and investment activities, such as in dealing in certain transferable securities or money market instruments, sanctions screening may also involve screening for those activities. A firm should have effective, up-to-date screening systems appropriate to the nature, size and risk of its business. Although screening itself is not a legal requirement, screening new customers, counterparties to transactions and payments against the UK Sanctions List, and screening existing customers when any amendments are made to the list, helps to ensure that firms will not breach UK sanctions. Screening polices 7.2A.7 Self-assessment questions: • If a customer was referred to your firm, how does the firm ensure the person is not designated? (Does the firm screen the customer against the list itself, or does it seek assurances from the referring party?) • Does your firm have a clear policy on which customers, counterparties and payments are subject to screening, and what related data is subject to screening? This may also include policies for screening related parties, including directors and ultimate beneficial owners. • Does your firm have a clear policy on what sanctions regimes it is seeking to screen against, and with what frequency? • If using an outsourced service, does your firm have appropriate control and oversight of its sanctions screening controls? • Has your firm documented its consideration of other forms of screening beyond name screening, such as for high-risk jurisdictions or services and goods? Examples of good practice Examples of poor practice • It is clear at what stage customers are screened in different situations (eg, when customers are passed from agents or other companies in the group). • A firm assumes that an intermediary has screened a customer, but does not check this. • Where exposure to trade sanctions risk is identified, the firm considers screening for restricted goods and services, high-risk ports and countries, and sanctioned vessels as well as designated persons. • A firm uses manual screening processes; however, the increasing size of its business has not been considered in its sanctions screening processes.

Asset freezing and licences 7.2A.12 When a financial sanction is an asset freeze, the funds and economic resources belonging to or owned, held or controlled by a designated person are generally to be frozen immediately by the person in possession or control of them, unless there is an exception in the legislation they can rely on, or they have a licence from OFSI. In addition to asset freezes, OFSI may issue licences for other sanctions measures, including sectoral sanctions and ancillary services bans. Relevant firms are required to report to OFSI, as soon as practicable, the nature and amount or quantity of any funds or economic resources they hold for a customer who is a designated person. Additionally, firms are required to report all frozen assets held for designated persons to OFSI annually, including details of all the funds or economic resources frozen in the UK as well as those overseas where the funds or economic resources are subject to UK financial sanctions legislation. For more information, see OFSI’s guidance on reporting. Self-assessment questions: • Does your firm have clear policies and procedures as to when funds and economic resources are frozen or released? • Have you assessed how any frozen funds and economic resources in your firm’s possession or control are maintained in compliance with UK sanctions? • Does your firm have clear policies and procedures to assess, utilise and monitor the use of OFSI licences and statutory exceptions? Reporting and assessing potential sanctions breaches 7.2A.13 Relevant firms are required to report to OFSI where they know, or have reasonable cause to suspect, a breach of financial sanctions, and notify OFSI if: • a person they are dealing with, directly or indirectly, is a designated person; • they hold any frozen assets; or • they discover or suspect any breach while conducting their business. Relevant firms are required to report to OTSI where they know or have reasonable cause to suspect a breach of trade sanctions and should additionally report to HMRC if the suspected breach relates to breaches of export controls and trade sanctions involving UK customs. In line with Principle 11, SUP 15.3.8G(2), SUP 15.3.11R(1) and FCG 7, firms must consider whether they need to notify us – for example, whether potential breaches of sanctions resulted from a significant failure in its systems and controls. Proliferation finance 7.2A.14 Alongside financial and trade sanctions, the government imposes controls on certain types of trade in order to achieve foreign policy objectives. The export of goods and services for use in nuclear, radiological, chemical or biological weapons programmes is subject to strict controls. Firms’ systems and controls and policies and procedures should address and mitigate the proliferation risks they face. Firms are also required to carry out proliferation financing risk assessments under regulation 18A of the Money Laundering Regulations, either as part of the existing practice-wide risk assessment or as a standalone document. Proliferation financing may utilise mechanisms similar to those used in sanctions evasion, and some proliferation finance measures are implemented through the use of targeted financial sanctions (including asset freezes). As a result, earlier sections of FCG 7 on sanctions risks are also relevant, including in relation to customer due diligence, risk assessments, screening, transaction monitoring and evasion detection. Self-assessment questions: • Does your firm finance trade with high-risk countries? If so, is enhanced due diligence carried out on counterparties and goods? Where doubt remains, is evidence sought from exporters that the trade is legitimate?

Case study – deficient sanctions systems and controls 7.2A.15 In October 2024, the FCA fined Starling Bank Limited £29m for financial crime failings related to its financial sanctions screening framework. • In January 2023, Starling identified that, since the implementation of its financial sanctions screening framework in 2017, its automated screening system had only been screening the names of new and existing customers against individuals on the Sanctions List with UK citizenship or UK residency. • A subsequent review of Starling’s financial sanctions framework identified wider systemic weaknesses, including deficiencies in its financial sanctions risk assessment, policies and procedures, the testing and calibration of screening systems, and a lack of effective management information on alert volumes and trends. • In addition, Starling breached a voluntary requirement (VREQ) restricting it from opening new accounts for high-risk customers, opening over 54,000 accounts for 49,000 high-risk customers between September 2021 and November 2023. Due to the breaches of the VREQ and Principle 3 of the FCA’s Principles for Businesses, the FCA imposed a financial penalty of £29m on Starling Bank Limited. For more information, see the FCA’s press release. Case study – OFSI imposition of monetary penalty – Citibank, N.A., London Branch 7.2A.16 In August 2026, OFSI imposed a monetary penalty of approximately £4.7m on Citibank N.A. London Branch for breaches of UK financial sanctions. The

FCA 202X/YY Page 63 of 67 case related to multiple transactions giving rise to breaches across Citibank N.A. London Branch’s operations, involving activity across a number of business areas and functions. This included payment processing, correspondent banking and account restrictions. OFSI’s assessment was that many of the breaches arose from specific systems and controls issues and/or errors by Citibank N.A. London Branch staff, or staff in the wider Citi group acting on its behalf. These issues arose in the context of the high volume of Russia-related sanctions designations following the invasion of Ukraine in 2022, which OFSI considered placed significant strain on the bank’s alert handling and investigation processes. In particular, delays in the review and escalation of sanctions alerts, and some instances of human error, appear to have contributed to the breaches. For more information, see OFSI’s Public Penalty Notice concerning Citibank, N.A., London Branch.
